talks.title: Security BSides 2024 // Alex Holden
talks.teaser: Traces the pro-Russian hacktivist group Killnet and how a research team disrupted it through a drug marketplace it relied on.
talks.summary:
Alex Holden, chief information security officer at Hold Security, looks at Killnet, a Russian hacktivist collective that started as a denial-of-service group in late 2021 and grew to a very large membership. Many members were IT professionals who had lost remote work for Western employers after 2022, and the group shifted toward attacks on Western government, corporate and healthcare targets, including a public call to attack hospitals in early 2023.

The middle of the talk follows how Holden's team traced the group's leadership and funding to an illegal online drug marketplace called Solaris. Analysts monitored drug platforms, where criminals reused nicknames, and used those overlaps to link actors to physical locations. The team later gained access to Solaris infrastructure after the marketplace's administrators asked them for help with a code problem, redirected marketplace payments to a Ukrainian charity, and published the stolen source code and data. The disruption hit the group's finances and leadership, leaving its membership far smaller.

Holden closes by arguing that the group's legacy is normalized activism, with members who did not hide their identities, and that propaganda now causes as much harm as breaches. In the questions he covered the legal review his team carried out and the personal risks, including threats and swatting attempts, that came with publicly naming the operation. The takeaway is that exposing an adversary's weak points can disrupt a large group, even though the threat remains active.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // Kurt Walton
talks.teaser: A police commissioner outlines cybercrime threats facing the Cayman Islands and the priorities for responding to them.
talks.summary:
Commissioner of Police Kurt Walton opens by describing his role in making the Cayman Islands safer, a mission that covers cybercrime as much as any other crime. He has spent well over 35 years in the Royal Cayman Islands Police Service and notes that the BSides event is in its third year. He thanks the speakers who presented earlier and points to the digital forensic hub's prevention and partnership approach.

He sets out three priorities: protecting the financial sector in an international finance centre, safeguarding personal information under local data protection rules with potential fines for breaches, and building awareness and skills across residents, businesses, schools and government. He also repeats three principles promoted by the digital forensic hub: complacency is the enemy of good security, nothing should be trusted without verification, and people should hold off when unsure.

On threats, he warns that organised groups use social media to reach large numbers of victims for romance fraud and confidence scams, often leading to fake cryptocurrency investments. He lists business email compromise, account takeover, phishing, malware that disrupts systems or steals data, ransomware, and exploitation of software flaws, and notes that cryptocurrency moved through mixers is hard to trace. Police have seen messages impersonating government agencies, financial institutions and energy companies seeking account details. He closes by calling for public and private sector partnerships and urging people to stop and think before responding to unexpected messages.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // Garry Coldwells
talks.teaser: Surveys IoT and OT risk across retail, healthcare and automotive, then how to gain asset visibility and automate response.
talks.summary:
This talk gives a broad view of Internet of Things security, focused on retail and healthcare with a shorter look at automotive. The speaker frames the problem as scale, with tens of billions of connected devices that often ship with default passwords, weak web and mobile interfaces, unencrypted communications and possible back doors. Past incidents serve as reference points: Stuxnet in 2010, the Mirai botnet in 2016, and the 2015 Jeep Cherokee case, where a compromised radio affected vehicle functions. The speaker also notes state-linked interest in operational technology.

The middle of the talk turns to architecture. Examples include a hospital campus rebuild planned with about 52,000 sensors in a single building and a Toronto property project with roughly 170,000 sensors. The proposed approach starts with knowing every device and its normal communication paths, then segmenting networks, applying least privilege and continuous monitoring. Endpoint, network, asset and identity tools should be linked through automated workflows, so that alerts lead to tickets, quarantine and remediation. The speaker cautions that API-based device management carries its own risk and that unmanaged devices still need visibility. A lifecycle model developed by an industry working group in Canada, with stages from define and discover through to refine, is presented as a way to structure the work.

The question round covered password habits, procurement standards, privacy of medical device data and residential solar systems, where a shared control module could create grid-level risk. The practical takeaways are to understand what each device talks to, bring procurement and change control in line with security standards, and assume that personal data may be exposed.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // Michael Castro
talks.teaser: Shows security leaders how storytelling, honest framing and supporting metrics can win over boards and staff.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security leaders often miss out on budget, support and understanding from executives and boards because they lead with technical facts rather than a story. It offers a four-part framework: understand your audience, be authentic, use metrics to support your narrative, and nurture a continuous security culture. Examples include a manager who wanted a monthly count of staff browsing pornography, and an ISO 27001 certification pitched to staff as a parent choosing a daycare. A Seinfeld clip and Apple's 1984 Super Bowl commercial show how stories make dry subjects land.

Authenticity means moving away from the fear, uncertainty and doubt tactics the speaker once used. Honest accounts work better, such as a denial-of-service attack where the team admitted it did not know when it would end but described its controls. Charts with unexplained dips needed context, so visuals should support the story, not replace it. Culture work means tying security to the business, as a grocery CEO's tomato remark showed, and speaking to each team in terms of its own work.

The closing advice is to decide the outcome first and work backwards, then earn enough trust that the audience listens.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // Will Baggett
talks.teaser: Applies an intelligence analyst's Carver framework to leaked ransomware group chats to rank what matters most to the attacker.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a Russian-linked ransomware group whose internal chat logs were leaked after the group publicly backed Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The speaker, a former military intelligence instructor, approaches the material the way an analyst would. He first explains how ransomware operations typically unfold: reconnaissance for sensitive data, compromised accounts, phishing, persistence, and deployment of the ransomware as the final step. He places the leak in wider context, covering earlier cyber and information operations around the conflict and how the leaked files were released and spread online.

The core of the talk is the CARVER targeting method, a scoring framework originally developed in World War II and used here to rank an organization's most important assets. Each asset is rated on criticality, accessibility, recoverability, vulnerability, effect and recognizability. Applied to the group, the speaker argues that its source code and developers rank highest, because credentials and staff can be replaced more easily than the core tooling. He then describes triage of the leaked data inside his own organization: checking for exposed credentials, typosquatted domains, phishing templates and indicators, and passing those findings to detection and leadership teams.

The closing section looks at insider threat. The speaker compares an internal leak to a gate opened on purpose, notes that a screenshot or copied file is hard for data loss controls to catch, and says slow patch cycles cannot keep pace with attackers. Takeaways include verifying leaked material before acting, checking your own exposure first, and documenting what you learn so others can use it.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // Mick Baccio
talks.teaser: Applies the SECI knowledge-creation model from 1980s auto manufacturing to how security teams share tacit and explicit knowledge.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the 1980s, when Japanese automakers such as Toyota and Honda took a large share of the US market from GM and Ford. The speaker links that gap to how knowledge moved inside organizations: rigid top-down hierarchies on one side, and continuous sharing of experience and documented procedures on the other. From there he walks through the SECI model, which describes how tacit knowledge and explicit knowledge convert into each other through socialization, externalization, combination and internalization.

Each stage is tied to a security example. A senior analyst passes on how to spot subtle patterns in network traffic, a team turns incident lessons into a response playbook, and an organization merges several threat feeds and logs into a threat model. The speaker presents frameworks such as the cyber kill chain and MITRE ATT&CK, along with ISACs, as ways of externalizing and sharing collective knowledge.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to build a culture of open collaboration, invest in mentorship, run post-incident reviews, and keep knowledge flowing across teams. In the question round, the speaker said AI tools need validation and do not hold tacit knowledge, and discussed why organizations hesitate to share incidents.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // CISO Roundtable
talks.teaser: Security leaders discuss AI adoption, diversity of thought, security culture and resilience in a CISO roundtable.
talks.summary:
A panel of security leaders, moderated by a consultant who advises small businesses, discussed how AI is being used by customers and in their own organisations. Panelists said adoption is often bottom up, and a government security chief described a light-touch process in which AI tools are assessed before they reach the government network, with AI-driven alert triage helping a small team stay effective. Another panelist called AI a force multiplier for understaffed teams and urged people to learn the tools now, comparing it to the earlier move to cloud.

On diversity, the panel argued that the goal is diversity of thought, which gender or background only hints at. Speakers suggested seeking talent deliberately, including through community colleges, and warned that mandated diversity may not feel genuine. Culture was described as shared values set from the top, with one panelist drawing on Toyota's production system and its respect for workers and customers.

The closing segment turned to resilience. One panelist defined it as planning for the hit and practising recovery, while another framed it as architecting failover and preventing incidents in the first place. The panel ended by urging attendees to put people before technology and to look after their mental health.

talks.title: 2024 Security BSides // Sue Richards
talks.teaser: Shows how to make security awareness training relevant, interactive and ongoing instead of a yearly compliance chore.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that annual security awareness training, often driven by compliance rules, rarely changes behavior. The speaker, who works on compliance and project management, notes that regulated courses have fixed formats, while information security content leaves more room to experiment. A phishing test built around a sunglasses discount drew clicks from most staff, so the program switched to a fake email from a boss about a document typo, which got faster responses. Failed clicks were framed as practice rather than failure.

Much of the session was hands-on. Volunteers led short group exercises, introducing themselves, telling a story and demonstrating a tool, so attendees could compare which style felt engaging. The speaker then shared case studies: a staged insecure workstation with a password note and an unshredded bin, letting staff spot problems without being singled out; themed awareness days tied to holidays and music icons; and industry-specific messages, such as comparing password habits to controls on prescription pads for a pharmacy client. A false-positive alert was also revisited as if it were a real attack, which helped right-size the response.

The closing advice was to make training continuous, using monthly phishing exercises, short regular newsletters, and office hours where staff can ask anything, including questions about personal devices. The speaker recommended finding advocates in other departments, visiting offices in person, and hosting informal events that build awareness into the invitation and logistics. The takeaway is to keep content relevant to each business, fun, and frequent, and to keep what works.

talks.title: Len Noe
talks.teaser: A live walkthrough shows how paid lookups and OSINT tools stitch public data into a convincing digital persona.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames identity as the overlap of physical traits, digital footprints, and countless online accounts, then defines synthetic identity as a modeled picture of behaviors, interests, and posts rather than a single stolen record. Everyday leaks, loyalty programs, and app permissions are positioned as fuel for targeted fraud and analytics at scale.

The core demonstration runs the speaker’s own identifiers through BeenVerified, then parallel scans with iknowyou, SpiderFoot, and Blackbird on a work email and the hacker213 handle. Results surface addresses, relatives, employment, many third-party accounts, and counterfeit social profiles built without hacking. The talk ranks major platforms by breadth of collection, cites 2022 fraud markets for documents, and shows ChatGPT summarizing family names, a podcast nickname for grandchildren, and prior speaking activity when fed those findings.

Closing guidance treats personal data like an attack surface: patch home gear, refuse unnecessary PII, avoid personality-quiz harvesting, prefer adaptive multi-factor authentication over bare two-factor, harden self-service recovery answers so OSINT cannot replay them, and extend zero-trust verify-everywhere thinking from enterprise architecture to individual digital lives.

talks.title: Will Baggett - DFIR: Analyzing Voting Machines at DefCon
talks.teaser: Explains how forensic examiners imaged and validated used voting machines at DEF CON, and what the evidence did and did not show.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how the DEF CON Voting Village examines used voting machines bought on secondary markets. It frames the work around impartial reporting and strict handling rules, with the aim of reporting what was found and what was not, and of producing results that another examiner could replicate.

It walks through an early case in which an older Windows XP machine with a 1997 Microsoft Access voting database was given to the examiner. The logs contained an FTP transfer to an outside server, even though the machine was supposed to have never been online, and that finding drew wide press attention. Examiners then built a repeatable workflow: write-blocked forensic images, hash validation, several duplicate copies, cross-checking with more than one tool, and filtering out known-good system files using published hash sets. A newer prototype with a camera, biometric capture, and cellular and Bluetooth links was also examined, including a chip-off extraction of its circuit board, and its output was written to an unencrypted text file on removable USB drives.

Across the machines examined over five years, the speaker reports no evidence of foreign or domestic interference and no malware. The talk points to weaknesses that still matter, such as a shared admin account, unencrypted output, and missing audit trails. For practitioners, the takeaways are to keep chain of custody tight, validate results with a second tool, and report only what the evidence supports. The talk closes with free tools and training options for newcomers to digital forensics.

talks.title: Andrés Vega - Policy as [versioned] code - you’re doing it wrong.
talks.teaser: Shows how to express compliance policy as versioned code that teams can test, depend on, and update like software.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that compliance rules usually live in documents and spreadsheets, which leads to case-by-case exception requests and teams guessing what a policy means for their systems. The speaker proposes treating policy as software: stored in version control, published with release notes, signed, and versioned with semantic versioning so every change is visible to the people who depend on it.

To show this, the speaker walked through a prototype repository with Terraform and Kubernetes examples. A first policy version required a department label on all resources, backed by tests. A later version turned that field into a fixed list, corrected a spelling mistake in one option, and added a new department. Consumer projects declared which policy version they depended on, and automated dependency updates opened pull requests to move them forward, so compliance status could be measured. For Kubernetes, policies were evaluated through admission controls, and several policy versions could be loaded at once.

The main takeaways are that each policy should carry its rationale alongside the code, so teams debate exceptions on reasons rather than negotiating them one by one, and that tooling alone is not enough: people, training and culture have to change as well. Keeping policy secret is hard to sustain and can hide the controls teams need to understand.

talks.title: John Watson
talks.teaser: Shows how a police digital forensics team traces fraud websites and phishing links, then takes them offline.
talks.summary:
A digital forensics team from a Cayman Islands police service explains how it handles cybercrime on the island. The speaker outlines the unit's work: extracting data from seized devices under a chain of custody, assisting investigations of crimes enabled by computers, and investigating crimes that can only be committed with a computer. He notes that the cases reaching his team are mostly online investment scams and phishing, and that organisations rarely report incidents to them.

The middle of the talk walks through several cases. A fake trading platform took large sums from one victim; tracing the operator through a listed address, a phone number and a company registry led nowhere, so the team had the page taken offline instead. A phishing email sent to government staff led to a page that looked like a genuine Microsoft login, and a network capture showed the password being sent to a third party before the real login page appeared. A later scam posed as a police refund service for people already defrauded by Ponzi schemes, supported by fake reviews on video-sharing sites. In each case the team disrupted the site rather than identifying the people behind it.

The talk closes by framing the community as a centre of gravity, arguing that criminals are driven by money and that law enforcement faces limits in foreign jurisdictions. The practical takeaways are to report incidents, to prepare incident response before a ransomware attack because outside help is usually needed, and to share intelligence across partners. Planned steps include an online reporting form, a group of responders for the community, and exercises with an external agency that has agreed to help.

talks.title: Vlad Logvinov - Board Reporting for the “IT Guy” 101
talks.teaser: Walks IT staff through structuring board reports, from risk registers and incidents to training metrics and progress over time.
talks.summary:
The talk is aimed at IT staff who suddenly have to report to a management committee or a board, often without a template to start from. The speaker says his team began building such reports a few years ago after a local regulator started asking for them. He argues that the presenter should first understand the audience's technical background, patience and available time, and should tie every point back to business impact such as risk, financial, regulatory and reputational effects. Reports should be simple, backed by statistics, free of jargon, and should offer short-term and long-term fixes, with improvement shown from one meeting to the next.

For structure, the speaker suggests starting with the risk register and showing only high and medium risks, with their residual ratings and named owners so that questions can be sent to the right people. He uses an approved exception, storing sensitive company ownership files on USB keys, as an example of a risk a board can explicitly accept. An incident section should appear even when it is empty, and can include near misses such as whaling emails or brand impersonation. Penetration test findings, along with remediation status, should be reported at least annually. Phishing results can start with open and click rates, and awareness training can report correct and incorrect answers and participation, without naming individual employees.

For the remaining areas, he suggests firewall and intrusion detection statistics, such as attack counts and quarantined malware, and help desk resolution rates broken down by department or application. Progress can be quantified through completed vendor assessments, infrastructure upgrades and the number of policies reviewed. To keep boards engaged, the speaker recommends varying the format over time and sharing recent industry cases, such as a deepfake voice fraud that led to a large transfer, to show why callback procedures matter.

talks.title: Ira Winkler
talks.teaser: Security researchers investigate Ira Winkler and analyze defensive countermeasures.
talks.summary: Ira Winkler keynotes at Cayman Connect by mapping scuba diving’s fatality-resistant ecosystem onto cyber security. He recounts personal near-misses—rock surf, dolphin pens, jellyfish lagoons—and ties them to layered training, instructor quality control, insurance, and incident investigations that expect human error. He rejects feel-good awareness without consequences, urging continuous nudges, role-appropriate training, and infrastructure that assumes users will click. PADI-style standards, cue cards, medical screening, and agency discipline become metaphors for embedding security across HR, IT, and leadership rather than annual checkbox videos.

talks.title: Discussion - Hacking Diversity: building A culture of Diversity and Inclusion
talks.teaser: Panelists explain how employers can attract and keep a more diverse security workforce, from job posts to mentoring.
talks.summary:
The panel, held at BSides Cayman Islands, looked at how organisations can attract, build and keep a diverse cybersecurity workforce. Panelists started with hiring. Long lists of required qualifications, they said, discourage many women from applying, and one regional employer reported more strong applicants after moving some requirements into a desirable-extras category. Small firms, they added, depend on leaders who truly believe in diversity.

Discussion then turned to culture and advancement. Speakers argued that a culture shaped by one narrow group excludes others, and that education, awareness and visible role models must come first. Equity was distinguished from equality, meaning extra support for people who start from a different place. Career changers were advised to create opportunities through mentoring, volunteering and skills from other fields, while paid study, remote work and employee network groups were cited as practical supports.

The closing remarks stressed that hiring one diverse person does not finish the job, and that leaders should check their own teams and build pipelines through schools and communities. Neurodiverse people were named as an underrepresented group whose thinking suits security work. The panel ended by asking attendees to note one action they could personally take.
